title: Dynamic routing: RIP, OSPF and BGP
summary: Three protocols, three philosophies. Understand distance-vector, link-state and path-vector, then focus on OSPF fundamentals while knowing what RIP and BGP are for.

sections.heading: Why dynamic routing exists
sections.html:
Static routes do not react. In a network with redundant paths, a failed link must be noticed and the table updated automatically, typically in under a second. That is what a routing protocol does: it exchanges reachability information, computes best paths, and reconverges after change.

The three families differ in what they exchange:

FamilyExchangesComputesExamples
Distance-vectorDistance to each destination (hop count)Bellman-Ford: trust your neighbour's claim plus one hopRIP, EIGRP (hybrid)
Link-stateOwn links and costs, flooded to everyoneDijkstra SPF over a complete topology mapOSPF, IS-IS
Path-vectorFull AS path to each prefixPolicy choice based on path attributesBGP

The consequence: distance-vector routers know only what their neighbours tell them ('the network is 3 hops that way'), so they can be misled — the basis of count-to-infinity loops. Link-state routers build an identical map of the whole area, so their decisions are consistent and convergence is faster, at the cost of memory and flooding.

sections.heading: RIP: the teaching protocol
sections.html:
RIP (Routing Information Protocol) is the simplest distance-vector protocol: maximum hop count 15, updates every 30 seconds, full table exchange with neighbours. Hop count ignores bandwidth — a 1 Gbps path and a 64 kbps path two hops shorter are treated as better.

It survives in exams and small labs, and in jobs mainly as a historical reference and a source of interview questions. Anti-loop mechanisms to know: split horizon (do not advertise a route back out the interface you learned it from), poison reverse (advertise it as unreachable instead), and triggered updates (send immediately on change).

RIPv2 added classless prefixes (CIDR) and authentication. RIPv1 was classful, which is why it appears in older material.

sections.heading: OSPF: the enterprise interior protocol
sections.html:
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is link-state. Core concepts:

ConceptMeaning
AreaGroup of routers sharing a topology database; area 0 is the backbone. All areas connect to 0.
LSALink state advertisement — the units of topology information flooded within an area.
LSDBLink state database: every router in an area has the same one.
CostInterface metric, by default reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth.
NeighbourAdjacent router, formed via Hello packets.
DR/BDRDesignated router on a broadcast segment, to limit adjacencies.

OSPF discovers neighbours with Hello packets on 224.0.0.5 (protocol 89, not TCP/UDP). Routers flood LSAs so every router has the same LSDB, then each runs Dijkstra to compute shortest paths to every prefix — nodes and links, not just hop counts.

Why it is the enterprise standard: fast convergence, no hop limit, supports VLSM and summarisation, and areas bound the flooding domain. In an interview, being able to say why one is better than RIP (fast, has loop-free topology computation, can weigh bandwidth) matters more than CLI details.

sections.heading: BGP: the internet's routing protocol
sections.html:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is path-vector and runs between autonomous systems: an AS is a network under one administrative control with a single routing policy (an ISP, a cloud provider, a large enterprise). BGP exchanges routes over TCP port 179 — the only one of these three that uses TCP.

Key terminology: AS path (the list of ASes a prefix traverses), eBGP vs iBGP (between ASes vs inside one), next hop, local pref, MED, and prefix filter.

BGP does not compute a shortest path in the OSPF sense. It selects by a long list of policy attributes where the AS path length is only one factor, and where policy — which peers you prefer, which prefixes you accept — dominates. That is the crucial difference: BGP is how the internet implements business relationships.

Consequences worth knowing: a BGP misconfiguration can black-hole a country's traffic (a leaked more-specific route wins by longest prefix match); route hijacking is possible without RPKI; and convergence is slow, measured in seconds to minutes, which is why a BGP flap is a serious event.

sections.heading: Choosing in practice
sections.html:
EnvironmentTypical choiceWhy
Linux host with two uplinksStatic routes, or BGP from the host in serious deploymentsSimple, no protocol overhead; BGP when the upstream requires it
Small office LANStatic or OSPFLittle redundancy, few routers
Enterprise campus/data centreOSPF or IS-ISFast convergence, scalability with areas
Between organisations / ISPBGPPolicy, AS-level control, scale

On Linux you can run frr (FRRouting) for OSPF and BGP, or keep hosts on static routes and let the routers handle dynamic protocols. The bird daemon is a lighter option. Neither is required for this application's exercises.

checks.prompt: Which protocol is link-state and computes shortest paths with Dijkstra?
checks.explanation: OSPF floods link state and each router runs SPF over an identical topology database. RIP is distance-vector and BGP is path-vector.

why_wrong.3: RIP uses hop count and Bellman-Ford.
why_wrong.2: BGP selects by policy attributes across ASes.
why_wrong.1: ARP is a link-layer address resolution protocol, not a routing protocol.

checks.prompt: Which protocol runs over TCP port 179?
checks.explanation: BGP peers over TCP 179. OSPF runs directly over IP (protocol 89) with its own multicasts; RIP uses UDP 520.

checks.prompt: Compare distance-vector, link-state and path-vector routing, and say where each is appropriate.

checklist.text: Distance-vector exchanges distance to destinations and trusts neighbours (RIP: hop count, max 15).
Link-state floods link information so every router has the same topology and runs SPF (OSPF, IS-IS).
Path-vector exchanges AS paths and applies policy (BGP), used between autonomous systems.
Mentions that hop count ignores bandwidth and that link-state converges faster with more resources.
Concludes with where each is used: RIP/labs, OSPF enterprise, BGP between ISPs.

checks.reference: Distance-vector protocols such as RIP share 'network X is N hops away' and apply Bellman-Ford, so they converge slowly, suffer count-to-infinity without split horizon, and cannot weigh bandwidth. Link-state protocols such as OSPF flood link information, so each router builds an identical map and computes shortest paths with Dijkstra — faster convergence and loop-free topology decisions at the cost of memory and flooding. Path-vector protocols such as BGP exchange complete AS paths between autonomous systems and choose by policy, which is how the internet expresses commercial and operational relationships. In practice: RIP is educational, OSPF/IS-IS inside an organisation, BGP between organisations.

connect.title: Longest prefix match
connect.text: Every protocol's output feeds the same table, and the same longest-prefix rule decides; that is how a leaked more-specific can hijack traffic.

connect.title: OSPF areas and VLANs
connect.text: Areas bound flooding, VLANs bound broadcasts — the same containment idea at different layers.

connect.title: Troubleshooting
connect.text: A routing problem shows up as 'reaches some destinations, not others' — and ip route get localises it in one command.

interview.q: What is the difference between OSPF and BGP?
interview.a: OSPF is an interior link-state protocol used inside an organisation: it floods topology data within areas and computes shortest paths by cost, converging in seconds. BGP is an exterior path-vector protocol used between autonomous systems: it exchanges AS paths over TCP 179 and selects routes by policy attributes rather than pure shortest path.

Because it is policy-driven with global blast radius: a misconfigured or leaked announcement can attract traffic by longest-prefix match, there is no built-in authentication (RPKI helps), and convergence is slow. A single bad export can black-hole a large address range.
